extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in sociology/psychology of crowds; legislators and statesmen seeking practical insight
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic study of the psychological characteristics, causes, and consequences of crowds (mass behaviour), emphasising what transforms assemblies into 'psychological crowds' and how to interpret or influence them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological law of the mental unity of crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: When individuals become an organised (psychological) crowd their sentiments and ideas turn in one definite direction and their conscious personality vanishes; the aggregation forms a collective mind (a 'single being') with clearly defined characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every numerical gathering is a psychological crowd — organisation and predisposing causes matter. A crowd's mental unity is transitory but produces new, determinable collective features. Example: thousands isolated may acquire crowd-qualities under strong shared emotions; an entire nation can become a crowd without physical aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical strength alone does not create a psychological crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere agglomeration of people (e.g., a thousand individuals accidentally side by side) does not constitute a psychological crowd; special predisposing causes are necessary for the assembly to acquire crowd characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware equating size with psychological unity. Analysts should look for shared direction of thought/sentiment and loss of individual personality before labelling an assembly a crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappearance of conscious personality / anonymity and loss of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals in a crowd often lose their sense of personal responsibility and conscious personality; anonymity generates a sentiment of invincible power that permits yielding to instincts normally restrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predict greater impulsivity and morally/legally transgressive acts when anonymity and perceived collective power are present. Anti-pattern: assuming individual moral restraints persist unchanged inside crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion (emotional and behavioral contagion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentiment and act in a crowd is contagious to a high degree; contagion is a hypnotic-like phenomenon whereby feelings, impulses and actions spread rapidly among members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contagion operates by reciprocity — shared suggestion strengthens itself. Practical implication: emotions and slogans spread rapidly; controlling initial signals can shape outcomes. Example: crowd members readily sacrifice personal interest to collective interest due to contagion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestibility / hypnotic-like state
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals immersed in a crowd enter a state resembling hypnotic fascination: conscious discernment and will are diminished, medullar/spinal activities predominate, and they become highly susceptible to suggestions directed at the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat crowd-directed appeals as 'suggestions' rather than rational arguments. The same suggestion gains force because it is shared by many; leaders and symbols thus have outsized influence. Anti-pattern: relying on detailed reasoning to change crowd opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowering of intelligence; predominance of unconscious/racial qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: In crowds, intellectual aptitudes and individuality are weakened; unconscious, inherited qualities common to a race (instincts, passions, sentiments) dominate, producing decisions that are mediocre rather than expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect inferior deliberative capacity from crowds — collective decisions often reflect average/common instincts rather than specialist insight. Example: assemblies of experts can still produce mediocre outcomes when functioning as crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of new collective characteristics (not an arithmetic average)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregation in a crowd does not simply average individual characteristics; rather, the combination can create wholly new properties (analogous to chemical combination) that differ qualitatively from the traits of constituent individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should look for emergent properties (new behaviors, passions, norms) rather than assuming the crowd equals the sum or mean of its members. This explains sudden collective acts not predictable from isolated individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneous vs homogeneous crowd effects / importance of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: While psychological crowds share general characteristics, particular traits depend on the crowd's composition (heterogeneous = mixed elements; homogeneous = similar elements as in sects, classes), which can modify its mental constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify crowds by composition to predict particular behaviors. Homogeneous crowds may amplify specific shared beliefs; heterogeneous crowds show common crowd traits plus particularities from constituent groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predisposing causes and stimuli determine crowd formation and direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain predisposing causes and exciting influences (race, traditions, intensity of emotion, leadership) are necessary for a crowd to form and to determine the direction its feelings and acts will take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate underlying causes (historical, cultural, emotional triggers) when diagnosing crowd behaviour. Policy-makers should identify and address these predisposing factors to anticipate or modulate crowd responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds are quick to act but mainly destructive in large-scale social change
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are characterised by rapid action and can be as heroic as criminal; historically they have often been the agents of the destruction of decaying civilisations rather than their constructive creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect crowds to excel in immediate, forceful action but to lack the foresight, discipline, and institutional continuity required for constructive, long-term societal organisation. Use caution before entrusting sustained constructive tasks to crowd-based processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical influence on policy: appeal to impressions, not pure reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and institutions have limited effect on crowds; to influence them effectively one must produce impressions that seduce them rather than appeal to pure equity or abstract reason (illustrated by the tax example: indirect, less-visible taxes are more easily tolerated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design public policy and communication to address perceptions and immediate impressions. Anti-pattern: implementing theoretically fair but highly visible measures that outrage crowd sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability by race, national genius and cultural inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd psychology varies with the hereditary qualities and 'genius' of a race or people; leaders and analysts must account for national characteristics to predict responses (e.g., Napoleon misjudged Spanish and Russian crowds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalise a crowd model across different cultures without adjustment. Historical and racial/ethnic inheritances shape how crowds respond to stimuli and leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective unconscious forces can originate complex cultural products
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite their unconscious nature, crowds can produce extraordinarily complex, organised phenomena (e.g., language) that surpass what isolated intellectuals could invent; the unconscious genius of crowds contributes to cultural creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that not all crowd effects are negative or unintelligent; some cultural creations and stable norms emerge from long-term unconscious collective activity. Analysts should distinguish immediate impulsive crowd acts from slow, unconscious mass processes that generate institutions or language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders of crowds and their means of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd leaders and the means they employ (symbols, slogans, authoritative posture) are decisive in shaping crowd suggestions and directions; effective leadership exploits suggestibility and contagion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the rhetoric, symbols, and emotional triggers used by leaders to understand or forecast crowd movement. Anti-pattern: assuming only formal arguments persuade crowds; in practice symbolic and emotional appeals dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious or ritual form adopted by crowd convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Convictions and beliefs of crowds tend to assume a religious or ritual shape, acquiring dogmatic and sovereign force beyond rational critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect crowd-held beliefs to be resistant to abstract criticism once they take on ritual or quasi-religious form. Persuasion efforts should account for this dogmatic character (use symbolism, ritualized messaging rather than dry logic).
